question: Which statement best describes a project, as opposed to business as usual?
options: A set of repeating daily tasks that carry on indefinitely
A unique, temporary piece of work with a set timeframe, goals to meet and a desired outcome
A unique piece of work with no deadline that carries on indefinitely
A set of recurring tasks with a set timeframe and a desired outcome

question: Which of these is an example of business as usual rather than a project?
options: Implementing a new customer relationship management (CRM) system by a deadline
Building a booking website for a parachuting school over three months
A level 2 support engineer resolving tickets escalated from level 1 support every day
Launching an online store as part of a digital transformation

question: What is a programme?
options: A single large project that spans several years
A group of unrelated projects run by different companies
A detailed plan of the tasks inside one project
An overarching umbrella of multiple related projects, which can span several years

question: Why did the instructor use the NHS Test and Trace programme as an example?
options: To show that programmes always succeed when they are well funded
To show that a project can be repeated exactly if the same team runs it again
To show the importance of effective project management, because failures can affect people's lives
To show that technology matters more than people in a programme

question: Which is the correct order of the five project lifecycle stages?
options: Planning, initiation, execution, monitoring and control, closure
Initiation, planning, monitoring and control, execution, closure
Initiation, execution, planning, monitoring and control, closure
Initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, closure

question: In which stage are the objectives and requirements identified and the overall project scope defined?
options: Planning
Execution
Initiation
Closure

question: Creating a budget, developing a work breakdown structure and producing a schedule happen in which stage?
options: Planning
Initiation
Execution
Monitoring and control

question: Formal acceptance, delivering the final product and reviewing lessons learnt happen in which stage?
options: Monitoring and control
Execution
Initiation
Closure

question: What is the purpose of the monitoring and control stage?
options: To carry out the actual work, usually overseen by a project manager
To define the overall scope and objectives of the project
To formally hand over the final product and review lessons learnt
To check the project is going according to plan by tracking performance

question: In the parachuting school activity, the developers wanted to start writing code straight away. Why couldn't they?
options: Initiation comes first to define objectives, requirements and scope, and detailed planning follows before the work is executed
Code can only be written after the project has been closed
Developers are not stakeholders, so they cannot start work
The whole programme must finish before any project can begin

question: Which consideration at the initiation stage covers legal and data protection requirements such as GDPR, and security?
options: Resource planning
Success metrics
Stakeholder analysis
Compliance

question: What does resource planning involve at the initiation stage?
options: Producing a detailed budget and a full work breakdown structure
A basic check of whether there is enough money, personnel and technology, with the detailed budget left to the planning stage
Measuring how successful each project has been after delivery
Identifying the risks and the strategies to mitigate them

question: Which of these belongs in the planning stage rather than the initiation stage?
options: A detailed budget plan
Stakeholder analysis
A risk assessment with mitigation strategies
Success metrics for each project

question: In the triple constraint triangle, which element did the instructor say is non-negotiable?
options: Time
Quality
Cost
Scope

question: A project is running out of time and the deadline cannot move. Which two options did the instructor give?
options: Reduce the quality or extend the deadline
Spend more on resources such as people or compute, or reduce the scope to the critical features
Reduce the scope or reduce the quality
Cut costs or reduce the quality

question: On a student's journaling-app project with an MVP deadline halfway through, what did the team do, as praised by the instructor?
options: Moved the deadline until every feature was finished
Dropped the critical features so the social features could ship first
Prioritised the critical features and pushed lower-priority ones, such as the social features, back until after the MVP
Added more developers so every feature was built by the deadline

question: Which set lists the four areas impacted by a project in the instructor's triangle?
options: Processes, products, technology and organisation
Processes, people, time and organisation
Policies, people, technology and operations
Processes, people, technology and organisation

question: Which best describes a stakeholder?
options: Anyone with an interest in, or who is impacted by, the project, even if they are not very interested
Only the people who fund the project
Only the developers who build the project
Only the customers who will use the end product

question: What does stakeholder analysis involve?
options: Listing everyone who works at the company
Deciding which stakeholders to remove from the project
Measuring how successful the project was for each stakeholder after closure
Understanding the stakeholders' needs, their level of interest and influence, and how much engagement the project needs from them

question: What is the correct order for stakeholder work in the initiation stage?
options: Analyse the stakeholders, identify them, then come up with strategies
Identify the stakeholders, analyse them, then come up with strategies to manage them
Come up with strategies, identify the stakeholders, then analyse them
Identify the stakeholders, come up with strategies, then analyse them

question: Why should stakeholder management strategies be reviewed during execution?
options: Because the list of stakeholders is fixed but the budget changes
Because strategies are only drafted once execution begins
Because regulators require a review every quarter
Because stakeholders' interest, influence and attitudes can change over time

question: Which two factors make up the power/interest grid used to analyse stakeholders?
options: Power (influence) and interest
Power and attitude
Interest and budget
Influence and cost

question: What approach applies to a stakeholder with high power and high interest?
options: A regular newsletter to keep them informed
Monthly briefings and occasional meetings
Monitoring them and updating them only on major developments
Constant, active management with regular detailed communication and involvement in critical decisions

question: What approach applies to a stakeholder with high power but low interest?
options: Watch them closely and inform them of major developments, because new information could raise their interest
Manage them closely with constant, active management
Ignore them completely, because they are not interested
Keep them informed with a newsletter and leave them out of decisions

question: What approach applies to a stakeholder with high power and only some interest (keep satisfied)?
options: Give them constant, active management with detailed daily updates
Keep them satisfied with less detail and less frequent meetings, such as milestone updates, but still give them a direct line for feedback
Send them a newsletter only and keep them out of decisions
Watch them silently and never contact them

question: What approach applies to a stakeholder with some power and some interest (keep on side)?
options: Give them constant, active management with daily meetings
Send them a newsletter and leave them out of all decisions
Keep them onside with monthly briefings and occasional meetings to get their input on decisions that affect them
Watch them and only contact them about major developments

question: What approach applies to a stakeholder with low power but some or high interest?
options: Keep them informed through newsletters, emails or large group meetings, without involving them in decisions
Give them constant, active management
Involve them in all the critical project decisions
Watch them closely in case their power grows

question: What did the instructor mean by 'ignore' for stakeholders with no power and no interest?
options: They are not ruled out: they are monitored lightly and kept informed through broad updates
They receive no communication of any kind
They are watched as closely as high-power stakeholders
They are given constant, active management

question: Why are regulators considered stakeholders?
options: They fund the project and decide its budget
They can set rules about how things must be done and stored, and can fine you if you do not follow them
They build the technical solution for the project team
They are the end users who will use the final product

question: How did the instructor describe competitors as stakeholders?
options: High power and high interest, so they should be managed closely
They are not stakeholders at all
Low direct power over the project, but they can still influence its direction, so they should be monitored
No influence of any kind, so they can be ignored

question: What did the instructor conclude about developers as stakeholders?
options: They are not stakeholders, because they only report to stakeholders
They have low power, so they should only be kept informed
The development team can be included as stakeholders with high power and interest, because they make many decisions about what is feasible
Only team leads count as stakeholders and developers should be excluded

question: Which is the correct order of stakeholder attitudes, from most positive to most negative?
options: Champion, supporter, critic, neutral, opponent, blocker
Champion, supporter, neutral, critic, opponent, blocker
Supporter, champion, neutral, critic, opponent, blocker
Champion, supporter, neutral, critic, blocker, opponent

question: What is the difference between a champion and a supporter?
options: A supporter actively works for the project's success, while a champion is in favour but not necessarily actively working towards it
A champion is neutral, while a supporter is a critic
A champion actively works for the project's success, while a supporter is in favour but not necessarily actively working towards it
There is no difference, because both actively work towards success

question: How did the instructor describe a critic?
options: Actively working to obstruct the project
On the fence, with no real opinion
Not in favour of the project, but not actively opposing it
In favour of the project, but not working towards it

question: What is the difference between an opponent and a blocker?
options: An opponent actively works to obstruct the project, while a blocker is actually obstructing progress
A blocker actively works to obstruct the project, while an opponent is actually obstructing progress
An opponent is neutral, while a blocker is a critic
There is no difference, because both only voice disagreement

question: How did the instructor suggest handling a stakeholder who persistently shows a bad attitude?
options: Remove them from the project immediately
Ignore them and hope their attitude changes
Start with a light touch, involve experienced people such as management or HR to bring them on side, and take firmer action if they persist
Move them to the 'ignore' box on the grid

question: In a personal development plan (PDP), what is the relationship between objectives and tasks?
options: Tasks are the goals, and objectives are the stepping stones towards achieving a task
Objectives are the goals, and tasks are the stepping stones towards achieving an objective
Objectives and tasks are the same thing under two names
Tasks are set by the client, and objectives are set by the learner

question: Which set correctly spells out SMART objectives?
options: Specific, measurable, attainable (realistic), relevant, time-bound
Specific, manageable, attainable, relevant, time-bound
Simple, measurable, attainable, relevant, time-bound
Specific, measurable, attainable, reliable, time-bound

question: What does SWOT stand for, as used to help identify PDP objectives?
options: Strengths, weaknesses, objectives, tasks
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats
Skills, weaknesses, opportunities, targets
Strengths, workload, opportunities, timeframes

question: Which structure did the instructor suggest for a 'tell me about yourself' answer?
options: Future, present, then past, with hobbies at the very start
Hobbies and interests first, then the future, with the past left out
A single hourglass structure applied to the whole answer
Past, present, then future, with hobbies and interests woven in and the future aspirations at the end
